title: Quadratic forms and cohomological invariants, Part II
summary: This continuation constructs higher quadratic Pfister theory in every characteristic, including nonsingular binary last factors and quadratic Witt modules in characteristic two. It proves roundness, the Arason–Pfister dimension bound and higher invariant criteria, then builds the non-dyadic henselian isotropy, finite Kronecker dimension and real-place descent arguments needed by Dittmann–Pop. Independent ordering-sensitive real function field applications are assigned to a separate proposed continuation.
readme: See research/blueprint/readmes/QuadraticFormInvariantsPartII.md for the definitive target statements, conventions, proof chains, definition APIs, discriminating tests, supplier contracts and the full routed-item assignment. All implementation statuses are unchecked. This draft plans Q2.0–Q2.7; the packet records two unresolved deep source/proof audits and exact supplier requests.

stages.title: Nonsingular forms and quadratic Witt modules in characteristic two
stages.description: Build the following target chain. On F² set [a,b](x,y)=a x²+xy+b y². Its polar matrix is [[2a,1],[1,2b]]; it is nonsingular exactly when 1−4ab≠0. Throughout, nonsingular means that the polar bilinear map has zero kernel; for these even spaces it agrees with Mathlib Nondegenerate. The hyperbolic plane is xy, including in characteristic two. For a field extension E/F and a finite-dimensional quadratic map q on V, construct q_E on E⊗F V by extending its degree-two coordinate polynomial. The result is independent of a basis and satisfies q_E(c⊗v)=c²q(v), with scalar extension of the polar form. Preserve nonsingularity, orthogonal sums and isometries; give coherent identity and tower isometries. For finite-dimensional nonsingular quadratic spaces over a field, split off hyperbolic planes until the complement is anisotropic. The anisotropic complement and Witt index are unique up to isometry; cancellation holds for an orthogonal nonsingular summand. Extend the existing odd-characteristic theorems to characteristic two, using xy for the hyperbolic plane. In characteristic two construct W_b(F), the Grothendieck ring of nonsingular symmetric bilinear spaces modulo metabolic classes; addition is orthogonal sum and multiplication is tensor product. Let I_b(F) be the kernel of dimension modulo two. Odd-characteristic W_b and I_b are imported from the parent roadmap through polarization; this node adds only the characteristic-two carrier and comparison interface. Construct I_q(F), the group of even-dimensional nonsingular quadratic spaces modulo hyperbolic spaces, with its W_b(F)-module action. For a symmetric bilinear form b and q, define b⊗q by its quadratic polynomial and the rule (b⊗q)(w⊗v)=b(w,w)q(v); its polar form is b⊗polar(q). The tensor is nonsingular when b and q are. A metabolic b or hyperbolic q acts by a hyperbolic tensor. Equal Witt class plus equal dimension implies isometry. For char≠2 identify I_q with the fundamental ideal of the imported Witt ring. For n≥1 put I_q^n(F)=I_b(F)^(n−1)·I_q(F) as subgroups of I_q(F). Thus I_q^1=I_q and I_q^(n+1)⊆I_q^n. In odd characteristic this is exactly the parent I(F)^n. There is no characteristic-two quadratic Witt ring whose n-th ideal power can replace this module filtration. Acceptance: [1,1] over F₂ is anisotropic and nonsingular. The proposed nonsingularity convention excludes odd-dimensional radical-free forms peculiar to characteristic two. The characteristic-two mixed coefficient is retained. Identity and composable field extensions commute up to the canonical tensor associator. Dimension 2m and Witt index m characterize hyperbolicity. No new odd-characteristic Witt decomposition is claimed. The identity is ⟨1⟩_b. A metabolic alternating plane has zero class even in characteristic two. The characteristic-two quadratic group is a module, with no unjustified product of two quadratic forms. Tensoring the bilinear line ⟨c⟩_b scales q by c. The exponent shift by one survives the n=1 test. The filtration and scalar extension commute by the tensor and quotient maps.

stages.title: Quadratic Pfister forms in every characteristic
stages.description: Build the following target chain. For n≥1 define an n-fold quadratic Pfister form as an (n−1)-fold bilinear Pfister tensor with a quadratic étale norm form. In char 2 its slots are a₁,…,a_(n−1)∈F× and a₀∈F, and its last factor is [1,a₀]; outer factors are ⟨1,−aᵢ⟩_b. In char≠2 use the existing n-fold parent construction with last factor ⟨1,−a₀⟩, a₀∈F×. The dimension is 2^n, the form represents 1, and its class belongs to I_q^n. Scaled n-fold forms generate I_q^n; unscaled forms generate additively for n>1. Do not assert the latter for n=1. The norm form of a quadratic étale F-algebra is round: its nonzero represented values equal its similarity factors. In char 2 the algebra F[t]/(t²+t+a) has norm [1,a]; in char≠2 F[t]/(t²−a) has norm ⟨1,−a⟩. The split algebra gives the hyperbolic case. If ρ is nonsingular and round then ⟨1,−a⟩_b⊗ρ is round, for a∈F×. For nonsingular ρ this tensor is isotropic iff it is hyperbolic iff a is a nonzero represented value of ρ, provided ρ is anisotropic; if ρ is already hyperbolic so is the tensor. Every n-fold quadratic Pfister form, n≥1, is round in every characteristic: D_F(ρ)=G_F(ρ) as subsets of F×. Import the parent one-fold and two-fold odd-characteristic cases and extend the induction to every length and to characteristic two. For a quadratic Pfister form ρ of length n≥1 over any field, isotropy, hyperbolicity, maximal Witt index 2^(n−1), and vanishing of its class in I_q(F) are equivalent. In odd characteristic reuse the existing length-two equivalence and prove the all-length extension. Acceptance: Zero terminal parameter in characteristic two gives a hyperbolic form. The empty outer list gives the binary norm form, never a one-dimensional quadratic form. Over F₂, [1,1] is the norm of F₄/F₂. Represented values and similarity factors here range over F×. The parameter test is conditional on anisotropic ρ. No division by 2 occurs in the tensor argument. The result is stable under arbitrary field extension. Zero belongs to the ordinary value image but is excluded from D_F and G_F. This equivalence is false for a general nonsingular isotropic quadratic form. In characteristic two use xy planes, not diagonal ⟨1,−1⟩.

stages.title: Polynomial representation and the Arason–Pfister bound
stages.description: Build the following target chain. If q is anisotropic over F then q_F(T) is anisotropic for a finite algebraically independent tuple T. Scalar extension I_q(F)→I_q(F(T)) is injective. For anisotropic q over F and h∈F[t] nonzero, if q represents h over F(t), there is a polynomial vector v∈V[t] with q(v)=h. The version with an additionally prescribed polynomial polar pairing with a fixed vector also holds. For anisotropic q,ψ over F, dim ψ=m, the following are equivalent: D(ψ_E)⊆D(q_E) for every extension E/F; the generic polynomial ψ(T) is represented by q_F(T); ψ admits an injective isometry into q. Consequently dim ψ≤dim q. For a finite field extension E/F and a nonzero F-linear functional s:E→F, transfer b and q by restricting scalars and composing their values with s. Transfer preserves nonsingularity and metabolic or hyperbolic forms and descends to W_b and I_q. It satisfies Frobenius reciprocity s_*(b_E⊗q)=b⊗s_*q. For E=F(θ) with θ≠0, use s(1)=1 and s(θ^i)=0 for 1≤i<[E:F]; its transfer of the one-fold bilinear Pfister class is ⟨⟨N_E/Fθ⟩⟩_b. An anisotropic quadratic form remains anisotropic under every finite extension of odd degree, in all characteristics. Hence restriction on I_q is injective for such extensions. For nonsingular even-dimensional q and a finite extension E/F, N_E/F(G(q_E))⊆G(q), with no characteristic restriction. Let q be nonsingular of even dimension over F and f∈F[T] nonzero. If q_F(T)≅f q_F(T), then q over Frac(F[T]/(p)) is hyperbolic for each irreducible p dividing f to an odd exponent. For nonsingular even-dimensional q over F and nonzero f∈F[T], a scalar multiple af with a∈F× is a similarity factor of q_F(T) iff q_F(p) is hyperbolic for every irreducible divisor p occurring oddly in f. Equivalently f* f is a similarity factor, where f* is the leading coefficient in the successive variable order used by EKM. For an anisotropic nonsingular quadratic form ψ of dimension m≥2, define F(ψ) as the degree-zero field of fractions of the integral graded ring Sym(V*)/(ψ), equivalently the function field of its projective quadric. Then ψ becomes isotropic over F(ψ). In dimension two this is the quadratic étale field attached to ψ; in dimension at least three nonsingularity makes the quadric geometrically smooth and anisotropy ensures the required integral equation. Define the generic point and its universal quadratic relation. Let q be nonzero anisotropic nonsingular, and ψ anisotropic nonsingular of dimension ≥2. If q_F(ψ) is hyperbolic, then for every a∈D(q), b∈D(ψ), the form abψ admits an injective isometry into q. In particular dim ψ≤dim q. For n≥1 and a nonzero anisotropic nonsingular quadratic form q with [q]∈I_q^n(F), dim q≥2^n. Equivalently a nonsingular form of dimension less than 2^n with class in I_q^n is hyperbolic. Acceptance: No infinitude assumption on F. Applies to characteristic-two nonsingular binary blocks. The output is a polynomial vector, stronger than a rational representation. The polar constraint supports binary block removal in characteristic two. In the nonsingular scope the characteristic-two binary blocks suffice. The result retains anisotropy of both forms. Separability is not required when using a nonzero functional. The zero functional is excluded. Purely inseparable odd-degree extensions are included. This is distinct from Springer complete-DVR anisotropy assigned to the real-function-field split. The norm is of a nonzero similarity factor. The functional is chosen as above, rather than assuming a separable trace. The complete DVR is an auxiliary proof device, not an assertion that the original valuation has rank one. This treats residue characteristic two because the integral polar form remains nonsingular. The statement fixes even dimension and nonsingularity. This is a theorem on actual similarity factors, not only a Witt relation. Do not take the full affine cone fraction field, which has an extra variable. For [1,1] over F₂ the field is F₄. All dimension comparisons use injective isometries. Anisotropy of q is essential. For n=1 the lower bound is 2, including characteristic two. The equivalent formulation permits isotropic q but concludes hyperbolicity below the strict bound.

stages.title: Higher quadratic cohomological invariants
stages.description: Build the following target chain. For n≥1 define the notation H_q^n(F)=H^n_et(F,Z/2(n−1)). If char F≠2 use continuous Galois cohomology with μ₂^(⊗(n−1)). If char F=2 interpret the coefficient complex by H_q^n(F)=H¹_et(F,Ω^(n−1)_log), using length-one logarithmic differentials and the shift by n−1. At n=1 this is H¹(F,Z/2), including the Artin–Schreier quotient in characteristic two. Import the coefficient objects, restriction and cup products from their existing owners; construct only the uniform notation/comparison adapter. When char F≠2, construct the surjective graded ring map s:K_*^M(F)/2→⊕ I(F)^n/I(F)^(n+1), sending {a₁,…,aₙ} to the imported parent n-fold Pfister class. Prove the Steinberg and multiplicativity relations; this construction establishes surjectivity, not injectivity. Fix a perfect k with char k≠2. On smooth k-schemes take the Zariski sheaf W associated to the Witt-group presheaf. For integral X with function field F put I^n(X)=W(X)∩I^n(F), and use the product over components for general X. Let i_n=I^n/I^(n+1), let k_n be the unramified mod-two Milnor sheaf, and set j_n=ker(k_n→i_n). Establish the 0-purity descriptions by intersections over codimension-one local rings and the residue/transfer cycle-module compatibility needed by Morel’s proof. These are sheaves built from the parent Witt functor, not another field Witt ring. In Morel’s induction fix N>0 and perfect k of characteristic ≠2. Assume s_n is an isomorphism for all fields over k in weights n<N, s_n(k) is an isomorphism for n≤N, and cup with τ=−1 makes H^(n−1)(F,Z/2(n−1))→H^(n−1)(F,Z/2(n)) surjective for every finite-type F/k and 1≤n<N. Then Ext^a_Ab(Sm_k,Zar)(k_n,j_N)=0 for 0≤n<N and a=0,1,2. For every field F of characteristic ≠2 and every n≥0 the Milnor homomorphism s_n:K_n^M(F)/2→I(F)^n/I(F)^(n+1) is an isomorphism, naturally in F. Composing its inverse with the separately imported norm-residue isomorphism gives I_q^n/I_q^(n+1)≅H_q^n(F) for n≥1. For char F=2 and n≥1 there is a natural additive isomorphism ē_n:I_q^n(F)/I_q^(n+1)(F)→H¹_et(F,Ω^(n−1)_log). On ⟨⟨a₁,…,a_(n−1),a₀]] it sends the class to the cohomology class represented by a₀ dlog(a₁)∧…∧dlog(a_(n−1)), equivalently the outer differential symbol acting on the Artin–Schreier character a₀. For a nonsingular quadratic n-fold Pfister form ρ, n≥1, define e_n(ρ)=ē_n([ρ] mod I_q^(n+1))∈H_q^n(F), using the odd-characteristic comparison followed by norm residue or the characteristic-two Kato comparison. It depends only on the isometry class. In odd characteristic it is the cup of the outer Kummer symbols with the final quadratic étale character; in characteristic two the last character is Artin–Schreier. For every field embedding F→E and quadratic n-fold Pfister form ρ, n≥1, res_E/F(e_n(ρ))=e_n(ρ_E), in the correctly twisted groups H_q^n. For a quadratic n-fold Pfister form ρ, n≥1, e_n(ρ)=0 iff ρ is isotropic iff ρ is hyperbolic. This holds over every field in the H_q convention. Acceptance: The wild target is H¹ of log forms, not the degree-n logarithmic sections themselves. BGK supplies logarithmic symbols; it does not by itself prove the quadratic graded-Witt comparison. The positive-degree map uses the same minus-sign Pfister convention as the parent. Injectivity is a separate theorem. Do not define i_n(X) as I^n(W(X)) on arbitrary schemes: the intersection construction is what is required. The field value of j_n is the kernel of the already named s_n. τ has motivic degree (0,1), rather than the Galois H¹ Kummer class of −1. The asserted vanishing is exactly the input for the extension-lifting construction. Two distinct deep inputs remain visible: quadratic Witt comparison and norm residue. Odd positive characteristic is covered by Morel, not by applying OVV4.1 outside its hypotheses. For n=1 recover the Arf/Artin–Schreier class of [1,a₀]. A square outer parameter gives a hyperbolic form and a zero dlog factor. Scalar-isometric presentations give the same invariant. The twist is n−1, matching the last Z/2 character. Composition of two field embeddings gives the same square. This includes inseparable characteristic-two embeddings. No claim that an arbitrary Witt-class invariant vanishes exactly on isotropic forms. The dimension argument uses n+1, rather than reapplying the bound at n.

stages.title: Non-dyadic henselian unit and value criteria
stages.description: Build the following target chain. Let w be a henselian valuation of arbitrary rank on F with residue field κ and (char F,char κ)≠(0,2). Let ε be the unit slots of a quadratic Pfister form. Then q_ε is isotropic over F iff q_ε̄ is isotropic over κ. Equal characteristic two is included. Under the unit-reduction hypotheses, if ε₁−1 has positive valuation then the two-fold q_(ε₁,ε₀) is isotropic, and every Pfister tensor containing it is isotropic. Require at least two slots. Under the unit-reduction hypotheses let π₁,…,π_s∈F× have F₂-linearly independent images w(π_i) in Γ/2Γ. Then q_ε̄ over κ, q_ε over F, and q_(π,ε) over F are isotropic simultaneously. The empty π-list is allowed. Acceptance: No rank-one, completeness, finite generation or finite residue field assumption. Mixed characteristic (0,2) is excluded; equicharacteristic (2,2) is allowed. In characteristic two the residual bilinear factor ⟨1,1⟩_b is metabolic. No assertion is made for a one-fold form with only a terminal principal unit. The argument uses only finitely many blocks and works for any ordered value group. Independence is in Γ/2Γ, not Γ⊗Q.

stages.title: C_i fields and finite Kronecker dimension
stages.description: Build the following target chain. For i≥0, a field F is C_i if every homogeneous polynomial of positive degree d in N>d^i variables has a nonzero zero over F. Zero polynomials count as homogeneous; degree zero is excluded. This is a property of actual polynomial evaluation, not a packaged existence assumption for quadratic forms only. Every finite field is C₁. For a homogeneous f of positive degree d<N, Chevalley–Warning makes the number of zeros divisible by the characteristic; the origin is a zero, so another zero exists. If F is C_i and f₁,…,f_r are homogeneous of the same positive degree d in N>r d^i variables, they have a common nonzero zero. If F is C_i then every algebraic extension E/F is C_i, including infinite algebraic extensions. If F is C_i and E/F has finite transcendence degree t, then E is C_(i+t). In particular a field of characteristic p>0 and finite absolute transcendence degree t is C_(t+1), and a finite-transcendence-degree extension of an algebraically closed field is C_t. For a field of finite absolute transcendence degree t, define δ(F)=t in positive characteristic and δ(F)=t+1 in characteristic zero. Prove δ(κ(w))<δ(F) for every nontrivial valuation w of such F. The relative algebraic closure of the prime field is called the constant field and has δ 0 or 1, respectively. Let F have finite δ(F)=r and a nontrivial non-dyadic henselian valuation with residue characteristic p>0. Any unit quadratic Pfister form of length r+1 is isotropic over F. Acceptance: The threshold is strict and degree positive. This owns the shared input for the real-function-field proposal. Applies to all finite prime-power fields. The argument counts solutions, so it gives more than the origin. The number of equations is part of the strict bound. This is not the unjustified claim that one-form C_i immediately handles systems. No finite-generation assumption on E itself. An algebraic extension does not increase the C_i index. The arbitrary algebraic tail is justified by coefficient descent. The real-function-field route imports the C_t conclusion and must separately connect C₁ to its Brauer-theoretic reduced norm input. δ(F_p)=0 and δ(Q)=1. An arbitrary valuation is allowed; no discrete-rank reduction. No condition involving real closures is needed in this case. Includes equal characteristic two; mixed (0,2) remains excluded.

stages.title: Coefficient fields and finite descent at real places
stages.description: Build the following target chain. For a henselian valued F with char F=char κ=0, construct a subfield E⊂O_w whose reduction E→κ is an isomorphism. E is relatively algebraically closed in F and contains the constant field k. If ε_i are units, lift their residues to η_i∈E×. Then ε_i/η_i are squares in F and the odd-characteristic Pfister forms q_ε and q_η are isometric. Let k′ be a number field and E′/k′ finitely generated of transcendence degree t with k′ relatively algebraically closed. At a finite place v let k′_v be its algebraic henselization; at a complex place use an algebraic closure. Then cd₂(E′k′_v)≤t+2 at finite places and ≤t at complex places. Thus H_q^m(E′k′_v)=0 for m>t+2. This does not assert cd₂(E′)<∞ if E′ has orderings. Let F,w be equicharacteristic-zero henselian of finite δ(F)=r, w nontrivial, with constants k and coefficient field E. Let q_η be a length r+1 Pfister form over E obtained from unit residues. If q_η is isotropic over Fk_v for every real closure k_v of k, there exists a finitely generated E′⊂E containing η such that, for k′=E′∩k, its invariant vanishes over E′k′_v for every place v of the number field k′. Let F have finite δ(F)=r and let w be nontrivial non-dyadic henselian, with no finite-generation hypothesis on F. Let ε be r+1 unit slots. If q_ε is isotropic over Fk_v for every real closure k_v of the constant field k, then q_ε is isotropic over F. The hypothesis is vacuous when k has no ordering. Acceptance: The coefficient field is a chosen section, not a canonical subfield. The square-lifting step requires residue characteristic zero. For t=0 the finite-place bound is 2. Finite-place algebraic henselization is distinguished from its analytic completion. The inverse-limit objects are finite sets of bad places, not Harrison spaces of all orderings. The composita and real closures are chosen compatibly; changing the choices transports the statement by field isomorphisms. The use of the Hasse principle occurs only in characteristic zero. The theorem includes arbitrary algebraic and non-finitely-generated extensions of finite-transcendence-degree fields.

stages.title: Patch-open henselization loci
stages.description: Build the following target chain. On Val_F=Spv(F), using the imported patch topology on valuation equivalence classes, let F_w^h denote a henselization. For every finite E/F, the locus of w admitting an F-embedding E→F_w^h is patch open. This is independent of the chosen henselization; a nonempty locus implies E/F separable. For every quadratic form q over F, the set {w∈Val_F : q becomes isotropic over F_w^h} is patch open. No nonsingularity, Pfister, characteristic or rank assumption is required. Acceptance: Use the existing valuation-spectrum quotient and topology. Only openness is asserted for the full union; individual witness neighborhoods are clopen. A one-dimensional anisotropic form may have the empty locus. An already isotropic form has the whole valuation spectrum as its locus.
